title: Help Understand Objective Angle and Subjective Angle

commenti.body:
Maybe there are differences between french (where I live) vocabulary and US ones, but when a critic or theoretician speaks of "subjective POV", it's almost always in a broad way. Because apart when you discover a place (face of someone watching > the landscape or place they see), it's rare that subjective POVs are really, literally, what you would see through their eyes. Because most of the time (specially in a conversation), it would be so weird it would break the immersion. When a films uses it, even with extra care and in a progressive way, it's still discusses as something unusual years after (*Silence of the lambs*, to keep to mainstream cinema).

When subjective POV is used in a film study, it's far more often for shots telling you that "it's the world as seen by this person", in a broad way. An usual example is the way, in the confession scene in *Eyes Wide Shut*, in which [Nicole Kidman is shown as suddenly freeing herself from the point of view of her husband](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=J7Z0AfpaM1U) (the change starting around 1'08): suddenly existing, her and her desire, outside of him. But the shots of her before that are not the literal POV of Tom Cruise. Who cares: it's her caught in a dialogue with her husband, nobody else can see her like that than him. And nobody is the room can see her in the way she start to appear after that.

Sure sometimes, when you want a stronger effect, literal POV can help to underline it. It's for instance the case in [the opening of *A separation*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=POIv4LpnxsA), during which you 100% adopt the POV of the judge, putting you right away in the place which will be yours: someone who will have to decide, in this film, who is guilty or not, because nobody will help you on that. But in that case, it works because it's an opening, it has a conceptual side which can work as an introduction. Not sure it would be doable in the middle of the film.

By coincidence Thomas Flight did a very interesting video essay on just this question a couple of days ago

"Why Perspective Matters So Much in Movies"

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qsxdFNaEqBk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qsxdFNaEqBk)

It might be helpful as it provides a number of illustrations of the theme from a number of sources.

Okay, so it’s a bit weird.

Typically objective and subjective reference to fact vs opinion/feeling. For example, the big park in New York City is called Central Park. That’s objective. But if you ask people what they think about Central Park, you’re getting subjective information. “It’s good.” “It’s scary.” “It’s full of trash.” “It’s so clean and comforting.” 

In writing, third-person voice tend to be objective, since it’s from an omniscient narrator. While first-person is subjective, as it’s a character speaking. However, limited third-person tends to be more subjective, as it’s restricted to the perspective of a singular character, despite being third-person. 

So true third-person might say “The wind blew from Boston, down to New York City, all the way to a small town in Ohio and across the face of Chris Lambert. Chris stood outside a coffee shop owned by the aunt of his neighbor. Eight hours from now, there will be a fire in the shop and Chris will be the prime suspect.”

First-person would go: “I hadn’t gone inside the coffee shop yet. Still didn’t know what to say. Even though Jenny was my neighbor and we grew up together, we never got along. Now she’s dead. And all I want is a cup of coffee but it’s Jenny’s aunt’s shop. And her aunt’s gonna be sad. She’s going to want to talk about Jenny. And I don’t. This wind is awful, though. Sharp. Frigid.”

And then limited-third is something like, “He parked his car and got out. The wind was immediate and pierced his jacket. He wanted that coffee now more than ever but stopped outside the door when he realized Jenny’s aunt, the owner, was probably the one working. The wind was no longer on his mind. Neither was the coffee.” 

You notice the more subjective nature of the limited. How much more similar it is to first than it is true third.

So cinematography can be similar. A wide shot of New York City is pretty objective. Shots within Central Park are pretty objective.  But if you see a bunch of people talking, laughing, doing various activities, and the camera goes weaving through them and around and captures some of the energy of being in the park—that’s more like limited-third and a bit more subjective. It’s trying to convey an emotion.

A POV shot, even though it’s from someone’s “subjective” perspective is still a bit objective because it’s simply showing you what someone is looking at. Not what they’re feeling when they look at it. 

That’s probably the key difference. Objective tends to just be “the thing” while subjective tends to get into a quality of the thing. 

You can think of it as an adverb. “He moved” is objective. “He moved slowly” adds in a qualitative element that’s a bit more open to interpretation. “I don’t think he moved all that slowly.” “Yeah, it seems more like he was moving deliberately than slowly.”

So the conversation example you gave. It’s not necessarily that you “feel” something because of the acting. It’s that the shots are done in a way that add to or change the emotional quality.

Like in 2001: a Space Odyssey, there’s the scene where Dave and Frank go to an escape pod to talk about maybe needing to shut down the sentient computer, HAL. The shots are very normal. But near the end, it cuts to close up of HAL’s “eye”, then reverses the shot to a close up of the lips of Dave and Frank. The camera moves from one to the other. We realize HAL’s been reading their lips this whole time and knows what they’re saying about it.

That’s “objective” in the sense that we’re simply seeing what HAL’s seeing. But it’s subjective because you suddenly feel in the scene and within all this emotion of what’s happening and the implication of the camera.

Another example would be a fight scene. If the camera stays back and has very few cuts, it’s more objective as we’re just bearing witness to the fight. 

If the camera shakes and is from a lot closer perspective and cutting between action and reaction—we’re in the action. We’re feeling more of the quality of the fight rather than observing it.

Spielberg might do something where the heroic protagonist receives a lot of close ups while the antagonist is often shot from medium to long distance. Why? Because the close up literally puts us closer to the hero. While the medium/long shot keeps us at a distance from the villain. That’s not done for observational reasons but in order to create an emotional response in a viewer.
Thank you for the long answer. Very Informative. Will take the time to understand it.

Sorry for still not understanding it but I have another question to give you a better perspective.


Massceli described Objective shots as beeing on the sideline, and Subjective Shots as like being on the field. But he also said that Subjective shots are strictly from the actual view of the player. So for example if you have a over the shoulder shot, that would still be objective, because it is not the actual vision of the player. It is still as like you, the viewer, is spectating the action as an unseen observer.
But now i am reading and watching about this topic and it is confusing, because now it is saying that the difference is, what you feel, not what you see.

For example an Close up of the player is filmed objectively, as i understand, but could be a subjective shot because you might feel the inner emotions of the player.
A scene can be filmed objectively because of not being the vision of the player, but is subjective because you feel the player.
This is so damn confusing and hard to understand.
